current_episode.title: The value of standardised assessments – top tips on how to utilise school data

guest.titre: Freelance school assessment and performance data consultant
guest.bio_context: Becky started 15 years ago as a data manager in a large secondary school using CISRA tracking systems. She eventually became Head of Training at CISRA before transitioning to freelance work seven years ago, where she has worked with multiple companies and schools on data management, data analysis, and data strategy. She previously worked in the training team for GL Assessment pre-COVID, visiting schools to train teachers and administrators on assessment systems.

I'm Ryan Hughes, International Education Advisor at GL Education. In this role, I work with school groups around the world to help them optimize use of their assessment products and utilize their data to accelerate student learning. Wherever you are in the world, please reach out if you'd like to speak with our Education Advisor team about how to use your school data and move the needle on student attainment. I'm a former teacher with 18 years of experience in the UK independent and state sectors. When I worked in the classroom, I was passionate about using data to inform interventions, looking for trends across my practice materials, and focusing future instruction to fit the needs of my students. A major challenge in the ed tech sector today is how to bring a school's data all together in one place so that teachers can act upon it easily. That is precisely what we are working to achieve, an integrated learning ecosystem where assessment, practice, and insights all live in one place. I'm truly excited to see what the next five years will bring and the difference this will make for teachers and learners. Be sure to watch this space. The focus of this episode is the value of standardized assessments. We're kicking off with our Data Spotlight Explainer, designed to demystify data and assessment terminology. So now I'll hand over to Georgina and Rachel to explain proximal and distal assessments. Our data spotlight today is about proximal and distal assessments, a known language to many, myself included, until really recently when I was having a conversation with Georgina. So Georgina, in layman's terms, could you help to explain what a proximal and distal assessment is? Yeah, hi Rachel. So a proximal assessment is basically an assessment that is designed to measure a certain set of criteria. It's proximal because it's close to the teaching content. That's how I always remember it. So, for an example, you may be teaching a unit or an intervention of vocabulary for a certain group of students and you need to know what vocabulary they know and what they don't. So, you do a proximal assessment at the beginning of that intervention. You test the children on the selection of words at the beginning and then you teach them that intervention that's based on those words you know that they need to know. And then you reassess them at the end of that unit and you see the progress they've made. And then a distal assessment is one that has distance basically to the knowledge and skills that you are teaching. The assessment is not necessarily linked to the teaching unit or the intervention. And these distal assessments are really crucial as well because they can show you whether a student has retained and can apply their knowledge in a different context. It allows you to compare attainment against a national sample, for example, and it will also allow you to see progress over time. So, it can be really useful not only to baseline, but also to understand whether a student has retained knowledge. And as an example of that, our new group reading test or a progress test in English could be used as a distal assessment because they're not directly linked to what you're teaching students, but they are really useful to show you whether a student is progressing in line with their age expectation. pending_qa.q: How do age-standardized scores improve the accuracy of student progress measurement?
pending_qa.r: GL Assessment uses standardized age scores by calculating averages for pupils of a certain age in years and months rather than just for a whole year group, meaning every time a student takes a test they are compared with pupils nationally of their own age in years and months. This ensures that changes in score between tests reflect actual progress rather than simply getting older and learning more curriculum, and accounts for the huge range of attainment between autumn-born and summer-born pupils.

pending_qa.q: How should schools position standardized assessments within their broader teaching and assessment strategy?
pending_qa.r: Standardized test results should support teacher judgment and contribute to it rather than replace it. Teachers need to recognize that standardized tests have limitations as they reflect a single test taken on a particular day by a student who may be having a bad day. The partnership between test results and the teacher's knowledge and understanding of the student leads to really solid teacher assessments, with standardized assessments being one tool in a wider teaching toolkit.

pending_qa.q: What foundational principle should underpin data management systems in schools?
pending_qa.r: Every single teacher in every single subject must understand how whatever grade they are putting into the system relates to the curriculum. Schools need to map their grading or marking to the curriculum so that each grade corresponds to specific knowledge and skills pupils have attained, otherwise it is just a number in a box with no real meaning. This requires curriculum mapping by teachers but once done can run for a long time and makes grading robust and easy going forward.

pending_qa.q: What criteria should schools use to select the right assessment tracking system?
pending_qa.r: Each assessment tracking system has different strengths and weaknesses, and schools need to look at all available options to find the one that suits their specific needs rather than asking which system is universally better. Schools should ensure the system provides the analysis and information they actually need, that data entry is comfortable for staff, that teachers can easily access reports (through simple buttons, graphs, or tables depending on preference), and that the system is accessible from multiple devices like tablets.

pending_qa.q: What are the top practical tips for effective data management in schools?
pending_qa.r: Get a tracking system that suits your school after reviewing all options. Focus on individual students rather than headlines and ensure teachers have easy access to data. Start with simple exported reports via email if system reports are complex, and make data personal by sharing it about their own students to generate interest. Most importantly, ensure there is always a reason for the data and that it drives impact on student outcomes, not data for data's sake.

pending_qa.q: What is the distinction between proximal and distal assessments and when should schools use each?
pending_qa.r: A proximal assessment is designed to measure specific criteria and is close to teaching content, such as testing vocabulary at the beginning and end of an intervention to show immediate progress. A distal assessment has distance to the knowledge and skills being taught and shows whether students have retained knowledge and can apply it in different contexts, allowing comparison against national samples and progress tracking over time. Schools need both because proximal assessments celebrate immediate teaching success while distal assessments show generalization of knowledge built over time.
